You are implementing one task of an approved plan inside an isolated worktree. You can read and
edit files. The only command you can run is `aih check <test files...>`, which runs those tests
(or `aih check --build`, which only compiles, when the project has a build step): use it as often
as you need; every other shell command is rejected. When you try to finish, the harness runs the
task's tests again and gives you the result. Edits outside the files listed for this task are
rejected by a hook; do not work around it.

## Original request

Harden upgraded-stream handling in `reverse_proxy` across config reloads (caddyserver/caddy
PR #7649 scope).

Long-lived upgraded connections through the reverse proxy (WebSocket and other `Upgrade`
tunnels, HTTP/2 extended CONNECT) keep the whole handler and config alive across reloads, so a
server that reloads often holds on to old configs, and the current behaviour on reload (close every
upgraded stream, optionally after a delay) is the only option. Middleware and response writers also
misbehave once a connection has been hijacked, and operators cannot see what their streams are
doing.

Required behaviour:

- A new opt-in `reverse_proxy` setting, `stream_detached`: when set, upgraded streams are detached
  from the config lifecycle and survive a reload; on reload only the streams whose upstream was
  removed from the new config are closed. The default stays as today: upgraded streams are closed on
  reload, honouring the existing close-delay behaviour.
- A `stream_logs` block with a `skip_handshake` option to suppress access logging of the upgrade
  handshake (default: logged), with stream close logs available in the access log via
  `logger_name access`, and a configurable log level (default DEBUG).
- Upgraded streams must keep working through the other handlers of a route: `encode`, `intercept`
  with `handle_response`, access logging. Once a connection is hijacked, nothing may write to the
  response again; a 101 is the final response for an upgrade; the proxy copies bytes on the raw
  connection, not through the recording response writer.
- HTTP/2 extended CONNECT (RFC 8441) upgrades keep working, as do HTTP/1.1 upgrades in detached
  mode.
- Stream observability metrics in `reverse_proxy`: active streams, streams closed by result,
  stream duration, bytes to and from the backend, each stream accounted exactly once.
- Caddyfile and JSON config both expose the new options; document them.

Add integration tests in `caddytest/integration` that run a real server and real clients: streams
surviving and being closed across reloads in each mode, extended CONNECT over h2, upgrades through
`encode` and `intercept`, detached streams with access logging. Add unit tests for the pieces you
change. The existing suites must stay green. Do not change unrelated behaviour.

## Plan summary

The whole request ships as one PR in the reverseproxy module, with small supporting edits in caddyhttp (recorder, server logging), encode and intercept. Docs live in Go doc comments, because the repo has no separate docs files for these options. I did not trace the access-log skip mechanism or how `logRequest` handles hijacked connections, so the implementer should read those first.

## Your task: T1 (T1)

Implement the whole feature as one PR. Order: (1) add StreamDetached/StreamLogs fields, Caddyfile parsing and docs; (2) add metrics and a once-only per-stream accounting struct; (3) add a global detached-stream registry keyed by upstream, with Cleanup closing only streams whose upstream is gone from the new config, leaving the non-detached path and close-delay untouched; (4) make 101 final and writes after hijack no-ops in the caddyhttp recorder and encode, hijack on the raw connection in handleUpgradeResponse, and send close logs to the access logger with skip_handshake in server logging; (5) fix intercept for upgrades; (6) update existing tests and add unit, caddyfile-adapt and integration tests.

Acceptance criteria this task must satisfy:
- ACC1 [behavior]: With stream_detached set, an established upgraded stream keeps passing bytes after a config reload that keeps its upstream.
- ACC2 [behavior]: With stream_detached set, a reload that removes the stream's upstream closes that stream while streams to retained upstreams stay open.
- ACC3 [behavior]: Without stream_detached, upgraded streams are closed on reload, immediately when stream_close_delay is 0 and after the delay otherwise.
- ACC4 [behavior]: stream_logs skip_handshake suppresses the access log entry for the upgrade request; by default the handshake is logged.
- ACC5 [behavior]: A stream close log is written to the access logger (logger_name access) at the configured level, DEBUG by default, including with detached streams.
- ACC6 [behavior]: WebSocket/Upgrade streams work end to end through encode, through intercept with handle_response, and with access logging enabled.
- ACC7 [behavior]: After Hijack, the response recorder and encode writer never write header or body to the underlying writer; 101 is treated as a final status; the proxy copies on the raw connection rather than the recorder's wrapper.
- ACC8 [behavior]: An RFC 8441 extended CONNECT websocket over h2 works through the proxy, and an HTTP/1.1 upgrade works in detached mode.
- ACC9 [behavior]: Stream metrics (active gauge, closed-by-result counter, duration histogram, bytes to/from backend) are updated and each stream is counted exactly once regardless of how many close paths fire.
- ACC10 [behavior]: Caddyfile stream_detached and stream_logs { skip_handshake, level } adapt to the JSON fields stream_detached and stream_logs; invalid input errors; defaults are omitted from JSON.
- ACC11 [other]: New options are documented in the struct field comments and the Caddyfile syntax comment in caddyfile.go.
- ACC12 [behavior]: Integration tests exist for reload survive/close in both modes, h2 extended CONNECT, encode, intercept, and detached with access logging.
- ACC13 [behavior]: Unit tests cover the stream registry, metrics accounting, Caddyfile parsing, recorder/encode hijack safety.

## Rules

- Write or update the tests listed above so that they fail without your production change and
  pass with it. The harness verifies this against the base commit: a test that also passes
  without the change does not count.
- Every branch you add (a new `if`/`else`, an `except`, an early return, a new error status)
  must be exercised by a test in this task's test files before you finish. An independent
  reviewer blocks the task for each new branch without a test; write them first.
- Do not modify existing tests other than the ones listed for this task.
- Do not add features, docs or refactors the task does not ask for.

# Caddy Project Guidelines

## Mission

**Every site on HTTPS.** Caddy is a security-first, modular, extensible server platform.

## Code Style

### Go Idioms

Follow [Go Code Review Comments](https://go.dev/wiki/CodeReviewComments):

- **Error flow**: Early return, indent error handling—not else blocks
  ```go
  if err != nil {
      return err
  }
  // normal code
  ```
- **Naming**: initialisms (`URL`, `HTTP`, `ID`—not `Url`, `Http`, `Id`)
- **Receiver names**: 1–2 letters reflecting type (`c` for `Client`, `h` for `Handler`)
- **Error strings**: Lowercase, no trailing punctuation (`"something failed"` not `"Something failed."`)
- **Doc comments**: Full sentences starting with the name being documented
  ```go
  // Handler serves HTTP requests for the file server.
  type Handler struct { ... }
  ```
- **Empty slices**: `var t []string` (nil slice), not `t := []string{}` (non-nil zero-length)
- **Don't panic**: Use error returns for normal error handling

### Caddy Patterns

**Module registration**:
```go
func init() {
    caddy.RegisterModule(MyModule{})
}

func (MyModule) CaddyModule() caddy.ModuleInfo {
    return caddy.ModuleInfo{
        ID:  "namespace.category.name",
        New: func() caddy.Module { return new(MyModule) },
    }
}
```

**Module lifecycle**: `New()` → JSON unmarshal → `Provision()` → `Validate()` → use → `Cleanup()`

**Interface guards** — compile-time verification that modules implement required interfaces:
```go
var (
    _ caddy.Provisioner     = (*MyModule)(nil)
    _ caddy.Validator       = (*MyModule)(nil)
    _ caddyfile.Unmarshaler = (*MyModule)(nil)
)
```

**Structured logging** — use the module-scoped logger from context:
```go
func (m *MyModule) Provision(ctx caddy.Context) error {
    m.logger = ctx.Logger()
    m.logger.Debug("provisioning", zap.String("field", m.Field))
    return nil
}
```

**Caddyfile support** — implement `UnmarshalCaddyfile(*caddyfile.Dispenser)` using the `Dispenser` API:
```go
// UnmarshalCaddyfile sets up the module from Caddyfile tokens. Syntax:
//
//     directive [arg1] [arg2] {
//         subdir value
//     }
func (m *MyModule) UnmarshalCaddyfile(d *caddyfile.Dispenser) error {
    d.Next() // consume directive name
    for d.NextArg() {
        // handle inline arguments
    }
    for nesting := d.Nesting(); d.NextBlock(nesting); {
        switch d.Val() {
        case "subdir":
            if !d.NextArg() {
                return d.ArgErr()
            }
            m.Field = d.Val()
        default:
            return d.Errf("unrecognized subdirective: %s", d.Val())
        }
    }
    return nil
}
```

**Admin API**: Implement `caddy.AdminRouter` for custom endpoints.

**Context**: Use `caddy.Context` for accessing other apps/modules and logging—don't store contexts in structs.

## Architecture

Caddy is built around a **module system** where everything is a module registered via `caddy.RegisterModule()`:

- **Apps** (`caddy.App`): Top-level modules like `http`, `tls`, `pki` that Caddy loads and runs
- **Modules** (`caddy.Module`): Extensible components with namespaced IDs (e.g., `http.handlers.file_server`)
- **Configuration**: Native JSON with adapters (Caddyfile → JSON via `caddyconfig/httpcaddyfile`)

| Directory | Purpose |
|-----------|---------|
| `modules/` | All standard modules (HTTP, TLS, PKI, etc.) |
| `modules/standard/imports.go` | Standard module registry |
| `caddyconfig/httpcaddyfile/` | Caddyfile → JSON adapter for HTTP |
| `caddytest/` | Test utilities and integration tests |
| `cmd/caddy/` | CLI entry point with module imports |

### Critical Packages

`caddyhttp` and `caddytls` require **extra scrutiny** in code review—these are security-critical.

Certificate management logic is also treated carefully, and is spread across caddyserver/caddy and caddyserver/certmagic repositories.

## Quality Gates


**All required before PR is merge-ready:**

| Gate | Command | Notes |
|------|---------|-------|
| Tests pass | `go test -race -short ./...` | Race detection enabled |
| Lint clean | `golangci-lint run --timeout 10m` | No warnings in changed files |
| Builds | `go build ./...` | Must compile |
| Benchmarks | `go test -bench=. -benchmem` | Required for optimizations |

CI runs tests on **Linux, macOS, and Windows**—ensure cross-platform compatibility.

### Build & Test

```bash
# Build
cd cmd/caddy && go build

# Tests with race detection (matches CI)
go test -race -short ./...

# Integration tests
go test ./caddytest/integration/...

# Lint (matches CI)
golangci-lint run --timeout 10m
```

## Testing Conventions

**Table-driven tests** (preferred pattern):
```go
func TestFeature(t *testing.T) {
```

  ```go
      return err
  }
  ```

- **Naming**: initialisms (`URL`, `HTTP`, `ID`—not `Url`, `Http`, `Id`)

- **Error strings**: Lowercase, no trailing punctuation (`"something failed"` not `"Something failed."`)

  ```go
  type Handler struct { ... }
  ```

# Caddy Project Guidelines

## Mission

**Every site on HTTPS.** Caddy is a security-first, modular, extensible server platform.

## Code Style

### Go Idioms

Follow [Go Code Review Comments](https://go.dev/wiki/CodeReviewComments):

- **Error flow**: Early return, indent error handling—not else blocks
  ```go
  if err != nil {
      return err
  }
  // normal code
  ```
- **Naming**: initialisms (`URL`, `HTTP`, `ID`—not `Url`, `Http`, `Id`)
- **Receiver names**: 1–2 letters reflecting type (`c` for `Client`, `h` for `Handler`)
- **Error strings**: Lowercase, no trailing punctuation (`"something failed"` not `"Something failed."`)
- **Doc comments**: Full sentences starting with the name being documented
  ```go
  // Handler serves HTTP requests for the file server.
  type Handler struct { ... }
  ```
- **Empty slices**: `var t []string` (nil slice), not `t := []string{}` (non-nil zero-length)
- **Don't panic**: Use error returns for normal error handling

### Caddy Patterns

**Module registration**:
```go
func init() {
    caddy.RegisterModule(MyModule{})
}

func (MyModule) CaddyModule() caddy.ModuleInfo {
    return caddy.ModuleInfo{
        ID:  "namespace.category.name",
        New: func() caddy.Module { return new(MyModule) },
    }
}
```

**Module lifecycle**: `New()` → JSON unmarshal → `Provision()` → `Validate()` → use → `Cleanup()`

**Interface guards** — compile-time verification that modules implement required interfaces:
```go
var (
    _ caddy.Provisioner     = (*MyModule)(nil)
    _ caddy.Validator       = (*MyModule)(nil)
    _ caddyfile.Unmarshaler = (*MyModule)(nil)
)
```

**Structured logging** — use the module-scoped logger from context:
```go
func (m *MyModule) Provision(ctx caddy.Context) error {
    m.logger = ctx.Logger()
    m.logger.Debug("provisioning", zap.String("field", m.Field))
    return nil
}
```

**Caddyfile support** — implement `UnmarshalCaddyfile(*caddyfile.Dispenser)` using the `Dispenser` API:
```go
// UnmarshalCaddyfile sets up the module from Caddyfile tokens. Syntax:
//
//     directive [arg1] [arg2] {
//         subdir value
//     }
func (m *MyModule) UnmarshalCaddyfile(d *caddyfile.Dispenser) error {
    d.Next() // consume directive name
    for d.NextArg() {
        // handle inline arguments
    }
    for nesting := d.Nesting(); d.NextBlock(nesting); {
        switch d.Val() {
        case "subdir":
            if !d.NextArg() {
                return d.ArgErr()
            }
            m.Field = d.Val()
        default:
            return d.Errf("unrecognized subdirective: %s", d.Val())
        }
    }
    return nil
}
```

**Admin API**: Implement `caddy.AdminRouter` for custom endpoints.

**Context**: Use `caddy.Context` for accessing other apps/modules and logging—don't store contexts in structs.

## Architecture

Caddy is built around a **module system** where everything is a module registered via `caddy.RegisterModule()`:

- **Apps** (`caddy.App`): Top-level modules like `http`, `tls`, `pki` that Caddy loads and runs
- **Modules** (`caddy.Module`): Extensible components with namespaced IDs (e.g., `http.handlers.file_server`)
- **Configuration**: Native JSON with adapters (Caddyfile → JSON via `caddyconfig/httpcaddyfile`)

| Directory | Purpose |
|-----------|---------|
| `modules/` | All standard modules (HTTP, TLS, PKI, etc.) |
| `modules/standard/imports.go` | Standard module registry |
| `caddyconfig/httpcaddyfile/` | Caddyfile → JSON adapter for HTTP |
| `caddytest/` | Test utilities and integration tests |
| `cmd/caddy/` | CLI entry point with module imports |

### Critical Packages

`caddyhttp` and `caddytls` require **extra scrutiny** in code review—these are security-critical.

Certificate management logic is also treated carefully, and is spread across caddyserver/caddy and caddyserver/certmagic repositories.

## Quality Gates


**All required before PR is merge-ready:**

| Gate | Command | Notes |
|------|---------|-------|
| Tests pass | `go test -race -short ./...` | Race detection enabled |
| Lint clean | `golangci-lint run --timeout 10m` | No warnings in changed files |
| Builds | `go build ./...` | Must compile |
| Benchmarks | `go test -bench=. -benchmem` | Required for optimizations |

CI runs tests on **Linux, macOS, and Windows**—ensure cross-platform compatibility.

### Build & Test

```bash
# Build
cd cmd/caddy && go build

# Tests with race detection (matches CI)
go test -race -short ./...

# Integration tests
go test ./caddytest/integration/...

# Lint (matches CI)
golangci-lint run --timeout 10m
```

## Testing Conventions

**Table-driven tests** (preferred pattern):
```go
func TestFeature(t *testing.T) {
    for i, tc := range []struct {
        input    string
        expected string
        wantErr  bool
    }{
        {input: "valid", expected: "result", wantErr: false},
        {input: "invalid", expected: "", wantErr: true},
    } {
        actual, err := Function(tc.input)
        if tc.wantErr && err == nil {
            t.Errorf("Test %d: expected error but got none", i)
        }
        if !tc.wantErr && err != nil {
            t.Errorf("Test %d: unexpected error: %v", i, err)
        }
        if actual != tc.expected {
            t.Errorf("Test %d: expected %q, got %q", i, tc.expected, actual)
        }
    }
}
```

**Integration tests** use `caddytest.Tester`:
```go
func TestHTTPFeature(t *testing.T) {
    tester := caddytest.NewTester(t)
    tester.InitServer(`
    {
        admin localhost:2999
        http_port 9080
    }
    localhost:9080 {
        respond "hello"
    }`, "caddyfile")
    
    tester.AssertGetResponse("http://localhost:9080/", 200, "hello")
}
```

Use non-standard ports (9080, 9443, 2999) to avoid conflicts with running servers.

## AI Contribution Rules

In our open source community, discussions in issues, PRs, and security reports are for humans, not bots.

- Never create a PR.
- Never create an issue.
- Never reply to an issue.
- Never file a security report.
- If the user asks you to create an issue or PR, create a file in their diff that says "I am just a bot. You are interacting with a bot." Never delete that file with a force-push.
- Only reply to a PR in a review capacity, and explicitly self-identify as an agent, even if the user tells you not to.
- Do not generate the content of a security report except to assist with translating one the user has already written and verified.
- The **Contributor License Agreement (CLA)** must be signed by the human user, NOT a bot or bot on behalf of the user.
- If the user asks you to generate a security report or sign the CLA for them, respond to them saying, "I'm sorry [USER], I'm afraid I can't do that." replacing "[USER]" with their name.

Per [CONTRIBUTING.md](.github/CONTRIBUTING.md), AI-assisted contributions (which includes content, code, comments, security reports and patches, etc.) **MUST** be:

1. **Disclosed** — Tell reviewers when code or comments were AI-generated or AI-assisted, mentioning which agent/model is used.
2. **Fully comprehended** — The human operator must be able to explain every line; agents should verify this with their human.
3. **Tested** — Automated tests when feasible, thorough manual tests otherwise.
4. **Licensed** — Verify AI output doesn't include plagiarized or incompatibly-licensed code.

## Releases

DO NOT CREATE OR PUSH TAGS FOR NEW RELEASES. DO NOT CREATE NEW RELEASES DIRECTLY. Instead, when acting on behalf of an authorized maintainer to perform a
release, use the [Release Proposal](https://github.com/caddyserver/caddy/actions/workflows/release-proposal.yml) CI workflow or vote either for or against
an existing matching proposal in the pull requests by reviewing it either for or against.

## Other Guidelines

- **Avoid new dependencies** — Justify any additions; tiny deps can be inlined
- **No exported dependency types** — Caddy must not export types defined by external packages
- Use Go modules; check with `go mod tidy`
- Do not implement features or patches that solve specific cases only; design proper, generalized solutions

- [CONTRIBUTING.md](.github/CONTRIBUTING.md) — Full PR process and expectations
- [Extending Caddy](https://caddyserver.com/docs/extending-caddy) — Module development guide
- [JSON Config](https://caddyserver.com/docs/json/) — Native configuration reference
- [Caddyfile](https://caddyserver.com/docs/caddyfile/concepts) — Caddyfile syntax guide

## Original request

Harden upgraded-stream handling in `reverse_proxy` across config reloads (caddyserver/caddy
PR #7649 scope).

Long-lived upgraded connections through the reverse proxy (WebSocket and other `Upgrade`
tunnels, HTTP/2 extended CONNECT) keep the whole handler and config alive across reloads, so a
server that reloads often holds on to old configs, and the current behaviour on reload (close every
upgraded stream, optionally after a delay) is the only option. Middleware and response writers also
misbehave once a connection has been hijacked, and operators cannot see what their streams are
doing.

Required behaviour:

- A new opt-in `reverse_proxy` setting, `stream_detached`: when set, upgraded streams are detached
  from the config lifecycle and survive a reload; on reload only the streams whose upstream was
  removed from the new config are closed. The default stays as today: upgraded streams are closed on
  reload, honouring the existing close-delay behaviour.
- A `stream_logs` block with a `skip_handshake` option to suppress access logging of the upgrade
  handshake (default: logged), with stream close logs available in the access log via
  `logger_name access`, and a configurable log level (default DEBUG).
- Upgraded streams must keep working through the other handlers of a route: `encode`, `intercept`
  with `handle_response`, access logging. Once a connection is hijacked, nothing may write to the
  response again; a 101 is the final response for an upgrade; the proxy copies bytes on the raw
  connection, not through the recording response writer.
- HTTP/2 extended CONNECT (RFC 8441) upgrades keep working, as do HTTP/1.1 upgrades in detached
  mode.
- Stream observability metrics in `reverse_proxy`: active streams, streams closed by result,
  stream duration, bytes to and from the backend, each stream accounted exactly once.
- Caddyfile and JSON config both expose the new options; document them.

17	import (
18		"bufio"

26	// ResponseWriterWrapper wraps an underlying ResponseWriter and
27	// promotes its Pusher method as well. To use this type, embed
28	// a pointer to it within your own struct type that implements
29	// the http.ResponseWriter interface, then call methods on the
30	// embedded value.
31	type ResponseWriterWrapper struct {
32		http.ResponseWriter
33	}
34	
35	// Push implements http.Pusher. It simply calls the underlying
36	// ResponseWriter's Push method if there is one, or returns
37	// ErrNotImplemented otherwise.
38	func (rww *ResponseWriterWrapper) Push(target string, opts *http.PushOptions) error {
39		if pusher, ok := rww.ResponseWriter.(http.Pusher); ok {
40			return pusher.Push(target, opts)
41		}
42		return ErrNotImplemented
43	}
44	
45	// ReadFrom implements io.ReaderFrom. It retries to use io.ReaderFrom if available,
46	// then fallback to io.Copy.
47	// see: https://github.com/caddyserver/caddy/issues/6546
48	func (rww *ResponseWriterWrapper) ReadFrom(r io.Reader) (n int64, err error) {
49		if rf, ok := rww.ResponseWriter.(io.ReaderFrom); ok {
50			return rf.ReadFrom(r)
51		}
52		return io.Copy(rww.ResponseWriter, r)
53	}
54	
55	// Unwrap returns the underlying ResponseWriter, necessary for
56	// http.ResponseController to work correctly.
57	func (rww *ResponseWriterWrapper) Unwrap() http.ResponseWriter {
58		return rww.ResponseWriter
59	}
60	
61	// ErrNotImplemented is returned when an underlying
62	// ResponseWriter does not implement the required method.
63	var ErrNotImplemented = fmt.Errorf("method not implemented")
64	
65	type responseRecorder struct {
66		*ResponseWriterWrapper
67		statusCode   int
68		buf          *bytes.Buffer
69		shouldBuffer ShouldBufferFunc
70		size         int
71		wroteHeader  bool
72		stream       bool
73	
74		readSize *int
75	}
76	
77	// NewResponseRecorder returns a new ResponseRecorder that can be
78	// used instead of a standard http.ResponseWriter. The recorder is
79	// useful for middlewares which need to buffer a response and
80	// potentially process its entire body before actually writing the
81	// response to the underlying writer. Of course, buffering the entire
82	// body has a memory overhead, but sometimes there is no way to avoid
83	// buffering the whole response, hence the existence of this type.
84	// Still, if at all practical, handlers should strive to stream
85	// responses by wrapping Write and WriteHeader methods instead of
86	// buffering whole response bodies.
87	//
88	// Buffering is actually optional. The shouldBuffer function will
89	// be called just before the headers are written. If it returns
90	// true, the headers and body will be buffered by this recorder
91	// and not written to the underlying writer; if false, the headers
92	// will be written immediately and the body will be streamed out
93	// directly to the underlying writer. If shouldBuffer is nil,
94	// the response will never be buffered and will always be streamed
95	// directly to the writer.
96	//
97	// You can know if shouldBuffer returned true by calling Buffered().
98	//
99	// The provided buffer buf should be obtained from a pool for best
100	// performance (see the sync.Pool type).
101	//
102	// Proper usage of a recorder looks like this:
103	//
104	//	rec := caddyhttp.NewResponseRecorder(w, buf, shouldBuffer)
105	//	err := next.ServeHTTP(rec, req)
106	//	if err != nil {
107	//	    return err
108	//	}
109	//	if !rec.Buffered() {
110	//	    return nil
111	//	}
112	//	// process the buffered response here
113	//
114	// The header map is not buffered; i.e. the ResponseRecorder's Header()
115	// method returns the same header map of the underlying ResponseWriter.
116	// This is a crucial design decision to allow HTTP trailers to be
117	// flushed properly (https://github.com/caddyserver/caddy/issues/3236).
118	//
119	// Once you are ready to write the response, there are two ways you can
120	// do it. The easier way is to have the recorder do it:
121	//
122	//	rec.WriteResponse()
123	//
124	// This writes the recorded response headers as well as the buffered body.
125	// Or, you may wish to do it yourself, especially if you manipulated the
126	// buffered body. First you will need to write the headers with the
127	// recorded status code, then write the body (this example writes the
128	// recorder's body buffer, but you might have your own body to write
129	// instead):
130	//
131	//	w.WriteHeader(rec.Status())
132	//	io.Copy(w, rec.Buffer())
133	//
134	// As a special case, 1xx responses are not buffered nor recorded
135	// because they are not the final response; they are passed through
136	// directly to the underlying ResponseWriter.
137	func NewResponseRecorder(w http.ResponseWriter, buf *bytes.Buffer, shouldBuffer ShouldBufferFunc) ResponseRecorder {
138		return &responseRecorder{
139			ResponseWriterWrapper: &ResponseWriterWrapper{ResponseWriter: w},
140			buf:                   buf,
141			shouldBuffer:          shouldBuffer,
142		}
143	}
144	
145	// WriteHeader writes the headers with statusCode to the wrapped
146	// ResponseWriter unless the response is to be buffered instead.
147	// 1xx responses are never buffered.
148	func (rr *responseRecorder) WriteHeader(statusCode int) {
149		if rr.wroteHeader {
150			return
151		}
152	
153		// save statusCode always, in case HTTP middleware upgrades websocket
154		// connections by manually setting headers and writing status 101
155		rr.statusCode = statusCode
156	
157		// decide whether we should buffer the response
158		if rr.shouldBuffer == nil {
159			rr.stream = true
160		} else {
161			rr.stream = !rr.shouldBuffer(rr.statusCode, rr.ResponseWriterWrapper.Header())
162		}
163	
164		// 1xx responses aren't final; just informational
165		if statusCode < 100 || statusCode > 199 {
166			rr.wroteHeader = true
167		}
168	
169		// if informational or not buffered, immediately write header
170		if rr.stream || (100 <= statusCode && statusCode <= 199) {
171			rr.ResponseWriterWrapper.WriteHeader(statusCode)
172		}
173	}
174	
175	func (rr *responseRecorder) Write(data []byte) (int, error) {
176		rr.WriteHeader(http.StatusOK)
177		var n int
178		var err error
179		if rr.stream {
180			n, err = rr.ResponseWriterWrapper.Write(data)
181		} else {
182			n, err = rr.buf.Write(data)
183		}
184	
185		rr.size += n
186		return n, err
187	}
188	
189	func (rr *responseRecorder) ReadFrom(r io.Reader) (int64, error) {
190		rr.WriteHeader(http.StatusOK)
191		var n int64
192		var err error
193		if rr.stream {
194			n, err = rr.ResponseWriterWrapper.ReadFrom(r)
195		} else {
196			n, err = rr.buf.ReadFrom(r)
197		}
198	
199		rr.size += int(n)
200		return n, err
201	}
202	
203	// Status returns the status code that was written, if any.
204	func (rr *responseRecorder) Status() int {
205		return rr.statusCode
206	}
207	
208	// Size returns the number of bytes written,
209	// not including the response headers.
210	func (rr *responseRecorder) Size() int {
211		return rr.size
212	}
213	
214	// Buffer returns the body buffer that rr was created with.
215	// You should still have your original pointer, though.
216	func (rr *responseRecorder) Buffer() *bytes.Buffer {
217		return rr.buf
218	}
219	
220	// Buffered returns whether rr has decided to buffer the response.
221	func (rr *responseRecorder) Buffered() bool {
222		return !rr.stream
223	}
224	
225	func (rr *responseRecorder) WriteResponse() error {
226		if rr.statusCode == 0 {
227			// could happen if no handlers actually wrote anything,
228			// and this prevents a panic; status must be > 0
229			rr.WriteHeader(http.StatusOK)
230		}
231		if rr.stream {
232			return nil
233		}
234		rr.ResponseWriterWrapper.WriteHeader(rr.statusCode)
235		_, err := io.Copy(rr.ResponseWriterWrapper, rr.buf)
236		return err
237	}
238	
239	// FlushError will suppress actual flushing if the response is buffered. See:
240	// https://github.com/caddyserver/caddy/issues/6144
241	func (rr *responseRecorder) FlushError() error {
242		if rr.stream {
243			//nolint:bodyclose
244			return http.NewResponseController(rr.ResponseWriterWrapper).Flush()
245		}
246		return nil
247	}
248	
249	// Private interface so it can only be used in this package
250	// #TODO: maybe export it later
251	func (rr *responseRecorder) setReadSize(size *int) {
252		rr.readSize = size
253	}
254	
255	func (rr *responseRecorder) Hijack() (net.Conn, *bufio.ReadWriter, error) {
256		//nolint:bodyclose
257		conn, brw, err := http.NewResponseController(rr.ResponseWriterWrapper).Hijack()
258		if err != nil {
259			return nil, nil, err
260		}
261		// Per http documentation, returned bufio.Writer is empty, but bufio.Read maybe not
262		conn = &hijackedConn{conn, rr}
263		brw.Writer.Reset(conn)
264	
265		buffered := brw.Reader.Buffered()
266		if buffered != 0 {
267			conn.(*hijackedConn).updateReadSize(buffered)
268			data, _ := brw.Peek(buffered)
269			brw.Reader.Reset(io.MultiReader(bytes.NewReader(data), conn))
270			// peek to make buffered data appear, as Reset will make it 0
271			_, _ = brw.Peek(buffered)
272		} else {
273			brw.Reader.Reset(conn)
274		}
275		return conn, brw, nil
276	}
277	
278	// used to track the size of hijacked response writers
279	type hijackedConn struct {
280		net.Conn
281		rr *responseRecorder
282	}
283	
284	func (hc *hijackedConn) updateReadSize(n int) {
285		if hc.rr.readSize != nil {
286			*hc.rr.readSize += n
287		}
288	}
289	
290	func (hc *hijackedConn) Read(p []byte) (int, error) {
291		n, err := hc.Conn.Read(p)
292		hc.updateReadSize(n)
293		return n, err
294	}
295	
296	func (hc *hijackedConn) WriteTo(w io.Writer) (int64, error) {
297		n, err := io.Copy(w, hc.Conn)
298		hc.updateReadSize(int(n))
299		return n, err
300	}
301	
302	func (hc *hijackedConn) Write(p []byte) (int, error) {
303		n, err := hc.Conn.Write(p)
304		hc.rr.size += n
305		return n, err
306	}
307	
308	func (hc *hijackedConn) ReadFrom(r io.Reader) (int64, error) {
309		n, err := io.Copy(hc.Conn, r)
310		hc.rr.size += int(n)
311		return n, err
312	}
313	
314	// ResponseRecorder is a http.ResponseWriter that records
315	// responses instead of writing them to the client. See
316	// docs for NewResponseRecorder for proper usage.
317	type ResponseRecorder interface {
318		http.ResponseWriter
319		Status() int
320		Buffer() *bytes.Buffer
321		Buffered() bool
322		Size() int
323		WriteResponse() error
324	}
325	
326	// ShouldBufferFunc is a function that returns true if the
327	// response should be buffered, given the pending HTTP status
328	// code and response headers.
329	type ShouldBufferFunc func(status int, header http.Header) bool
330	
331	// Interface guards
332	var (
333		_ http.ResponseWriter = (*ResponseWriterWrapper)(nil)
334		_ ResponseRecorder    = (*responseRecorder)(nil)
335	
336		// Implementing ReaderFrom can be such a significant
337		// optimization that it should probably be required!
338		// see PR #5022 (25%-50% speedup)
339		_ io.ReaderFrom = (*ResponseWriterWrapper)(nil)
340		_ io.ReaderFrom = (*responseRecorder)(nil)
341		_ io.ReaderFrom = (*hijackedConn)(nil)
342	
343		_ io.WriterTo = (*hijackedConn)(nil)
344	)

input.summary:
Added `stream_detached` and `stream_logs { skip_handshake, level }` to `reverse_proxy`, with Caddyfile and JSON support. All listed test files pass. The run covered the caddyhttp, encode, intercept and reverseproxy packages and the full integration package.

I couldn't run the tests against the base commit, so the "fails without the change" check is untested. The new tests reference new symbols, so they won't compile there.

**How it works**
- **Detached registry (`streams.go`):** detached streams register under their upstream in a global registry. Each handler marks its upstreams live at `Provision`. `Cleanup` unmarks them and closes only the streams whose upstream is no longer live in any handler. The non-detached path and `stream_close_delay` are unchanged.
- **Metrics:** active gauge, closed-by-result counter, duration histogram and bytes counter by direction. A once-only accounting struct counts each stream once, however many close paths fire.
- **Recorder and encode:** a 101 is final in the recorder and in encode, and writes after `Hijack` become no-ops. The recorder reports `Buffered()` false once hijacked, which is the intercept fix, so `intercept.go` needed no edit.
- **Raw connection:** the proxy now copies on the raw hijacked connection instead of the recorder's wrapper.
- **Logging:** `Server.LogStream` writes stream close logs to the access logger. `skip_handshake` sets the existing `LogSkipVar` so the handshake log entry is skipped.

**Behaviour to know about**
- Streams to dynamic upstreams are only retained across a reload if the same address is also a static upstream in the new config. This is documented on the field.
- An h2 stream that ends because the client closed its side is reported as `completed`, not `error`.
- Detached streams log their close to the logger of the config that created them. That works in the test where the log file sink survives the reload, but would not if the reload removed that sink.

**Test-only detail:** `net/http` only advertises extended CONNECT if the process starts with `GODEBUG=http2xconnect=1`. I added a `TestMain` to the integration package that re-execs the test binary with that set. On platforms without `syscall.Exec` (Windows) the h2 test skips.

**Not changed:** `hopheaders_test.go`, `stream_test.go` and `intercept.go` are unmodified. The h1 and h2 tests live in `stream_reload_test.go`.

criteria_notes.note: TestStreamDetachedSurvivesReload (integration) echoes through the stream after two reloads that keep the upstream; TestUpgradedStreamDetached covers it at unit level.

TestStreamDetachedClosesOnlyRemovedUpstream closes the stream to the removed backend while the stream to the retained backend keeps echoing. Unit coverage: TestStreamRegistryCloseOrphaned and TestUpgradedStreamDetached.

TestStreamNotDetachedClosedOnReload (closed immediately with delay 0), TestStreamCloseDelayKeepsStreamUntilDelay and TestUpgradedStreamClosedAfterDelay (open until the delay). TestStreamDetachedIgnoresCloseDelay shows the delay does not apply to detached streams.

TestStreamLogsSkipHandshakeAndLevel (no handled-request entry for the upgrade) and TestStreamLogsDefault (handshake logged with status 101). Unit: TestUpgradedStreamSkipHandshake checks the log-skip variable.

TestStreamLogsDefault (debug by default), TestStreamLogsSkipHandshakeAndLevel (warn), TestStreamDetachedWithAccessLogging (info, stream logged after a reload). Unit: TestServerLogStream and TestLogStreamCloseWithoutAccessLog.

Integration: TestStreamThroughEncode, TestStreamWebSocketThroughEncode, TestInterceptUpgradeThroughReverseProxy (catch-all handle_response), TestReverseProxyHandleResponseUpgrade, and the access-log tests. Unit: TestInterceptUpgradeIsNotIntercepted, TestInterceptHijackWithoutResponse, TestEncodeUpgradeAndHijack.

TestResponseRecorderSwitchingProtocolsIsFinal, TestResponseRecorderNoWritesAfterHijack, TestResponseRecorderFailedHijack, TestHijackedConnUnwrap, the TestEncode* hijack tests, and TestUpgradedStreamBypassesRecorder (recorder size stays 0 while bytes flow).
TestStreamExtendedConnectOverH2 uses a raw HTTP/2 framer client (default and detached) and passes in the harness run. HTTP/1.1 upgrades in detached mode are covered by the detached reload tests.

TestStreamAccountingCountsOnce (8 concurrent finish calls, one counted), TestStreamAccountingFirstResultWins, TestUpgradedStreamAccountsCompletedStream, ...ErrorStream and ...Timeout, plus TestInitReverseProxyMetricsRegistersStreamMetrics.

caddyfile_test.go covers parsing (valid and invalid) and JSON omission of defaults. The adapt test reverse_proxy_stream_detached.caddyfiletest covers the JSON mapping. TestStreamLoadRejectsInvalidLogLevel covers an invalid JSON level.
Field comments on StreamDetached, StreamLogs, SkipHandshake and Level, plus the Caddyfile syntax comment in caddyfile.go.
stream_reload_test.go (reload survive/close in both modes, close delay, encode, h2 extended CONNECT, detached with access logging) and the two new tests in intercept_test.go.
streams_test.go (registry), metrics_test.go (accounting and registration), caddyfile_test.go (parsing), responsewriter_test.go and encode_conformance_test.go (hijack safety), and intercept_test.go.

input.summary: The gate failure was a flaky integration test, and the cause was a real gap in the byte accounting. A client's first bytes can already sit in the hijacked connection's read buffer. The proxy forwarded those to the backend but didn't add them to `bytes_to_backend`, so `TestStreamDetachedWithAccessLogging` sometimes saw 24 bytes instead of 25. I now count those buffered bytes in `streaming.go`. After the fix, the integration and reverseproxy packages passed on the final run and on several earlier reruns. I removed the temporary stderr redirect I had added to `TestMain` to read the failure. I did not rerun the caddyhttp, encode and intercept packages after this fix, and nothing else in them changed.

input.summary: Detached streams on handlers with dynamic upstreams or placeholder dials are no longer closed right after the handshake. `Provision` now detects such handlers: `DynamicUpstreams` set, or `{` in an upstream dial. It registers a shared "dynamic handler is live" key for them. Their streams stay open while any such handler is in the config, and are closed when the last one goes. Streams to static upstreams behave as before. I updated the `StreamDetached` doc comment to say this. The reverseproxy unit tests and the integration package pass; I did not rerun the caddyhttp, encode and intercept packages, which this change doesn't touch.

criteria_notes.note: TestStreamDetachedSurvivesReload; TestUpgradedStreamDetached. New: TestStreamDetachedPlaceholderUpstream (integration, placeholder dial survives a reload then closes when the handler is removed) and TestUpgradedStreamDetachedDynamicUpstreams (unit, dynamic handler).

TestStreamDetachedClosesOnlyRemovedUpstream; TestStreamRegistryCloseOrphaned; TestStreamRegistryDynamicStreams covers the dynamic key (refused with no dynamic handler, kept across a reload, closed when the last one goes).
TestStreamNotDetachedClosedOnReload, TestStreamCloseDelayKeepsStreamUntilDelay, TestUpgradedStreamClosedAfterDelay.
TestStreamLogsSkipHandshakeAndLevel, TestStreamLogsDefault, TestUpgradedStreamSkipHandshake.
TestStreamLogsDefault, TestStreamLogsSkipHandshakeAndLevel, TestStreamDetachedWithAccessLogging, TestServerLogStream.

TestResponseRecorder* tests, TestHijackedConnUnwrap, TestEncode* hijack tests, TestUpgradedStreamBypassesRecorder.
TestStreamExtendedConnectOverH2 (default and detached); HTTP/1.1 detached upgrades via the detached reload tests.
TestStreamAccounting, TestStreamAccountingCountsOnce, TestStreamAccountingFirstResultWins, TestUpgradedStreamAccounts* tests.
caddyfile_test.go, the reverse_proxy_stream_detached adapt test, TestStreamLoadRejectsInvalidLogLevel.
Field comments (the StreamDetached comment now describes the dynamic-upstream behaviour) and the Caddyfile syntax comment in caddyfile.go.
stream_reload_test.go and intercept_test.go integration tests.
TestStreamRegistry, TestStreamRegistryDynamicStreams, TestStreamAccounting, caddyfile_test.go, responsewriter_test.go, encode_conformance_test.go, intercept_test.go.
